svg.aria-label: How an executable is cached and the kernel structures that describe it. Processes in two containers and on the host all execute the same binary by different paths; each path resolves to one inode, whose address_space holds one set of struct page entries in RAM, read in once from disk. Below, struct inode links by i_mapping to struct address_space, whose i_pages xarray maps a file offset to a struct page holding flags, a mapping pointer back to the address_space, and an index. Neither structure records who may write the page: permission is checked at the syscall boundary against the path the file was opened by, so a kernel subsystem handed the page pointer directly is checked by nothing. A closing strip traces the consequence: splice places such a page on the source side of a request, sg_chain carries it to the destination side, authencesn writes four bytes into it, and the cached code changes while the file on disk does not.
svg.title: The page cache, its structures, and their role in the vulnerability
svg.desc: Three bands. The upper band shows one cached executable shared by processes in two containers and on the host, reached by three different paths but resolving to a single inode and a single set of cached pages, read in once from the host filesystem. The middle band opens the two structures that describe that cache: struct inode, linked by i_mapping to struct address_space, whose i_pages xarray maps each file offset to a struct page recording flags, a mapping pointer back to the address_space, and an index — and neither structure records write permission, which is checked instead at the syscall boundary against the path used to open the file. The lower band names the four steps by which that omission is reached in Section 9.4: splice, sg_chain, the authencesn scratch write, and the resulting change to cached code that never touches disk.

g.text: one struct page per 4 KiB of the file
Different paths, different mount namespaces, different containers — the kernel resolves each to the same inode,
and serves every read, mmap and execve from these same pages. There is no per-container page cache: a namespace
virtualises the names by which objects are reached, and the page cache is not addressed by name.
THE TWO STRUCTURES THAT DESCRIBE IT
the page-cache index for one file
one physical 4 KiB frame of file data
